# Compactness below the quarter-mass threshold on the hollow double triangle

This proves a compactness result in every continuous dimension for the
fixed hollow projection
\[
 P=(2\Delta_2)\cap\mathbb Z^2
   =\{v_0,v_1,v_2,m_{01},m_{02},m_{12}\},
\]
where \(v_0=(0,0)\), \(v_1=(2,0)\), \(v_2=(0,2)\), and
\(m_{ij}=(v_i+v_j)/2\).

The argument uses elementary cone volumes rather than a mixed-volume or
dimension-flag classification. It does not prove the sharp depth bound
on this support. It shows that a sequence retaining a fixed strict depth
gap below that bound cannot escape all common affine normalizations.

## 1. A bounded-volume body containing a bounded positive-volume subset

**Lemma 1.** Suppose compact convex sets \(B\subset L\subset\mathbb R^d\),
\(d\ge1\), satisfy
\[
 B\subset R\mathbb B_d,\qquad |B|\ge v>0,
 \qquad |L|\le V,
\]
where \(R>0\). Then
\[
 L\subset R\left(1+\frac{2dV}{v}\right)\mathbb B_d. \tag{1}
\]

*Proof.* Fix \(x\in L\) with \(T=|x|>R\), and put \(u=x/T\).
Fubini gives
\[
 |B|=\int_{-R}^{R}
   \mathcal H_{d-1}(B\cap\{u\cdot y=s\})\,ds.
\]
The essential supremum of these section areas is at least \(v/(2R)\).
For a section at height \(s\), its convex hull with \(x\) lies in \(L\)
and has volume its base area times \((T-s)/d\). This pyramid formula
follows by integrating its homothetic sections. Taking section areas
arbitrarily close to their essential supremum yields
\[
 V\ge\frac{T-R}{d}\frac{v}{2R}.
\]
Rearrangement proves (1). In dimension one, the section measure is
\(\mathcal H_0\) and the same calculation is the length of an interval.
\(\square\)

The center of an inscribed ball in \(B\) is irrelevant to this lemma.
It needs only its bounded location and positive volume.

## 2. A volume-preserving normalization of one positive fiber

**Lemma 2.** A compact convex body \(K\subset\mathbb R^d\), of volume
\(a>0\), admits an affine map whose linear part has absolute determinant
one, such that
\[
 0\in K',\qquad
 K'\subset\sqrt d\,(d!a)^{1/d}\mathbb B_d. \tag{2}
\]

*Proof.* A maximum-volume inscribed simplex exists by compactness of
\(K^{d+1}\) and continuity of its determinant. Send its vertices to
\(0,e_1,\ldots,e_d\) by an affine map with absolute linear determinant
\(D\). Replacing its \(i\)-th vertex by any point of the transformed
body multiplies the simplex volume by the absolute value of that point's
\(i\)-th barycentric coordinate. Maximality implies that each coordinate
\(x_i\), \(1\le i\le d\), lies in \([-1,1]\). The transformed body
contains the standard simplex, so \(Da\ge1/d!\).

Multiply all continuous coordinates by \(D^{-1/d}\). The combined
linear determinant is one in absolute value, the selected simplex
vertex remains zero, and the containing cube has circumradius
\(\sqrt d D^{-1/d}\le\sqrt d(d!a)^{1/d}\). This proves (2).
\(\square\)

## 3. Uniform compactness under a uniform nonheavy margin

Let \(K_z\), \(z\in P\), be nonempty compact convex fibers forming an
actual convex family. In particular
\[
 (K_{v_i}+K_{v_j})/2\subset K_{m_{ij}}. \tag{3}
\]
Let their total mixed \(d\)-volume be \(M>0\). Fix \(q<1/4\), and assume
\[
 |K_z|\le qM\quad\hbox{for every }z\in P. \tag{4}
\]
Zero-volume fibers are permitted. If \(q<1/6\), this class is empty;
otherwise the following explicit bound applies.

**Theorem 3.** There is an admissible affine map
\[
 (z,x)\longmapsto(z,A x+Bz+b),\qquad A\in\operatorname{GL}(d,\mathbb R),
\]
such that the transformed mixed volume is one and every transformed
fiber belongs to a ball of radius depending only on \(d,q\).

*Proof.* First scale all continuous coordinates by \(M^{-1/d}\), so
that the total mass is one and every fiber mass is at most \(q\).
Write
\[
 v_*:=\frac{1-3q}{3}>0,\qquad
 v_{**}:=\frac{1-4q}{2}>0.
\]
The three midpoint fibers have total mass at most \(3q\), so one vertex
fiber has mass at least \(v_*\). Call it vertex zero for this proof; this
is only a relabeling of the three vertices and requires no change of
integer coordinates.

Apply Lemma 2 to that vertex fiber. Since its mass is at most \(q\), it
now contains zero and lies in \(R\mathbb B_d\), where
\[
 R=\sqrt d\,(d!q)^{1/d}.
\]
The map has absolute determinant one and does not change any mass.
Choose one point in each of the other two vertex fibers. An ordinary
affine shear in \(z\) sends all three chosen vertex points to zero and
leaves the normalized zero-vertex fiber unchanged: the three projection
vertices are an affine basis of \(\mathbb R^2\). Thus all three vertex
fibers contain zero. Equation (3) is preserved by this shear.

For each of the two incident midpoint fibers, (3) includes half of the
normalized vertex fiber. This subset is contained in
\((R/2)\mathbb B_d\) and has volume at least \(v_*/2^d\). Lemma 1 and
the midpoint mass upper bound \(q\) give
\[
 K_{m_{01}},K_{m_{02}}\subset T\mathbb B_d,
 \qquad
 T=\frac R2\left(1+\frac{2^{d+1}dq}{v_*}\right). \tag{5}
\]
Because zero belongs to the normalized vertex fiber, (3) also includes
\(K_{v_1}/2\) and \(K_{v_2}/2\) in these respective midpoint fibers.
Thus
\[
 K_{v_1},K_{v_2}\subset2T\mathbb B_d. \tag{6}
\]

The chosen vertex and all three midpoint fibers account for at most
\(4q\) of the unit total mass. Therefore the two remaining vertex
masses sum to at least \(1-4q\). One is at least \(v_{**}\); call that
one \(v_1\). The last midpoint contains \(K_{v_1}/2\), because the
other endpoint fiber contains zero. By (6), this subset is in
\(T\mathbb B_d\) and has volume at least \(v_{**}/2^d\). A second
application of Lemma 1 gives
\[
 K_{m_{12}}\subset
 T\left(1+\frac{2^{d+1}dq}{v_{**}}\right)\mathbb B_d. \tag{7}
\]

Equations (5)-(7) bound all six fibers. For example, one common radius is
\[
 R_*:=2T\left(1+\frac{2^{d+1}dq}{v_{**}}\right). \tag{8}
\]
All transformations fixed the integer coordinates, and their continuous
linear parts were invertible. They preserve the mixed-integer lattice
bijectively, send ambient halfspaces to ambient halfspaces, and multiply
all fiber volumes by one common factor. The total factor is \(M^{-1}\),
from the initial normalization alone. This proves the theorem. \(\square\)

The argument controls positions as well as diameters. It does not leave
any unbounded centroid displacement to be removed by a nonlinear
fiber-dependent translation.

## 4. Limits and maximum depth

For a sequence satisfying (4) with one fixed \(q<1/4\), apply Theorem 3
member by member. All six fibers are nonempty convex subsets of the
same compact ball, so a subsequence converges simultaneously in the
Hausdorff topology. Denote its limits by \(K_z^\infty\).

Actual compatibility is closed. For any barycentric representation of
an integer index, approximate chosen points in the limiting source
fibers by points in the original fibers, retaining the same barycentric
coefficients. Passing their convex combination to the limit places it
in the limiting target fiber. Thus the convex hull of the limiting
fibers has precisely those fibers at \(P\). There are no further
integer projection points because \(P\) is lattice-convex.

Volume is continuous for bounded compact convex sets under Hausdorff
convergence, including zero-volume limits. Therefore the limiting total
mixed volume is one. More precisely, the fiber indicator functions
converge in \(L^1\): for a full-dimensional limit, interior and exterior
points stabilize away from its null boundary; for a lower-dimensional
limit, the vanishing volume gives the assertion directly. Summing the
six differences proves total variation convergence of the mixed
measures.

Maximum normalized halfspace depth is continuous along this subsequence.
Here are the details needed for closed and oblique halfspaces. In one
fixed integer fiber, move a candidate from \(x\) to \(x'\). A nonvertical
containing cap may be written with unit continuous normal and boundary
through that candidate. Keeping its normal and integer coefficients
fixed changes every fiber threshold by at most \(|x-x'|\). Each fiber
lies in \(R_*\mathbb B_d\), so the intervening slab has volume at most
\(\kappa_{d-1}R_*^{d-1}|x-x'|\). Summing over six fibers gives a uniform
Lipschitz bound; use \(\kappa_0=1\) when \(d=1\). Vertical caps do not
change when the continuous candidate moves. Infima over these caps
retain the same bound. Total variation convergence changes each fixed
candidate depth by at most the total variation error.

To pass maxima, select maximizing candidates and take a subsequence
with fixed integer index and converging continuous point. Hausdorff
convergence places its limit in the corresponding limiting fiber, and
the preceding bounds give the upper-limit inequality. Conversely,
approximate a limiting maximizer in its fixed original fibers to get
the lower-limit inequality. Hence the maxima converge. No closed
halfspace carrying an entire boundary fiber was discarded.

## 5. Consequence for a fixed strict depth gap

For every positive-volume fiber, its ordinary centroid gives the
elementary heavy-fiber bound
\[
 \max_{y\in S}\operatorname{depth}_S(y)
       \ge\gamma_d\frac{|K_z|}{M}. \tag{9}
\]
Indeed every containing ambient halfspace cuts that fiber in a
centroid-containing continuous halfspace, or contains it entirely.
Classical Grünbaum supplies the indicated mass from that fiber alone.

Thus a uniform strict gap
\[
 \max\operatorname{depth}_S\le\frac{\gamma_d}{4}-\epsilon,
 \qquad\epsilon>0,
\]
implies (4) with
\[
 q=\frac14-\frac\epsilon{\gamma_d}<\frac14.
\]
Theorem 3 and Section 4 apply in every \(d\ge1\). Such a sequence cannot
escape all common \(\operatorname{GL}(d)\) maps and ordinary affine
shears while retaining that fixed gap. Merely assuming each fiber is
strictly below one quarter, without a uniform margin, does not supply
uniform constants in (8). In an escaping sequence the heavy-fiber bound
then forces the gap to vanish along the relevant subsequence.

## 6. Attainment and the possible zero-volume boundary

If the infimum of maximum depth over actual families on this fixed \(P\)
is strictly below \(\gamma_d/4\), choose a minimizing sequence within
some fixed strict sublevel. Its normalized subsequence is compact by
the preceding results, and depth continuity shows that the infimum is
attained. The same argument works in any fixed finite-facet class:
admissible affine maps preserve facet counts, and a positive-volume
Hausdorff limit of polytopes with at most \(N\) facets still has at most
\(N\) facets; zero-volume limits may be retained as such.

The mass proof yields more precise information about degeneracy. Along
a subsequence two fixed vertex fibers have the uniform lower bounds
\(v_*\) and \(v_{**}\). Each midpoint fiber contains half of at least
one of them, so all three midpoint fibers have volume at least
\(\min(v_*,v_{**})/2^d\). Therefore the only possible zero-volume fiber
is the remaining single vertex.

Deleting that possible zero-volume vertex preserves the measure and
maximum depth. Indeed, an integer-direction linear functional uniquely
maximized at that projection vertex gives a closed vertical halfspace
containing precisely its fiber. Its measure is zero, so every candidate
in the deleted fiber has depth zero. The other candidates and the
measure are unchanged. The retained family is still actual: its convex
hull is contained in the original convex hull and contains each retained
fiber, so none of those fibers changes; the deleted extreme projection
vertex cannot reappear. The
remaining integer projection has lattice width one: if the deleted
vertex is \((0,2)\), the remaining second coordinates are zero or one;
if it is \((2,0)\), use the first coordinate; if it is \((0,0)\), use
the primitive integer functional \(z_1+z_2\), whose remaining values are
one or two. This is an exact compactness/degeneracy alternative, not an
assumption of a general hollow-projection classification or a proof of
the sharp bound on the remaining width-one set.
